claim: Of the ~150,000 protein crystal structures in the public Protein Data Bank (PDB), ~122,000 (~81%) have a non-polymer ligand modeled.
source: Of the ~150,000 protein crystal structures in the public Protein Data Bank (PDB) (Berman et al., 2000), ~122,000 (~81%) have a non-polymer ligand modeled, and many thousands more reside in private pharmaceutical company databases.
evidence: Cites Berman et al., 2000 for the PDB and provides specific statistics about ligand-containing structures.

claim: Of the trove of public protein-ligand crystal structures, the vast majority (~94%) with temperature annotations were determined at cryogenic (cryo) temperature (≤200 K).
source: However, of the trove of public protein-ligand crystal structures, the vast majority (~94%) with temperature annotations were determined at cryogenic (cryo) temperature (≤200 K), typically after the protein crystals were flash-cooled in liquid nitrogen.
evidence: Provides specific percentage based on analysis of PDB structures.

claim: Only a small minority (~6%) of public protein-ligand crystal structures were determined at elevated temperatures (>200 K).
source: By contrast, only a small minority (~6%) were determined at elevated temperatures (>200 K; of these, mostly >277 K or 0°C).
evidence: Provides specific percentage based on analysis of PDB structures.

claim: Cryo crystallography distorts protein conformational ensembles.
source: Previous work has shown that cryo crystal structures of proteins have greater inherent variability than do RT structures, presumably due to idiosyncratic crystal cryocooling kinetics (Keedy et al., 2014).
evidence: Cites Keedy et al., 2014 as supporting evidence.

claim: Room-temperature (RT) crystallography reveals distinct protein conformational heterogeneity that better aligns with solution data and is in some cases more relevant to biological function.
source: This statistic is unnerving in light of the fact that, for proteins, cryo crystallography distorts protein conformational ensembles (Keedy et al., 2014), whereas room-temperature (RT) crystallography reveals distinct protein conformational heterogeneity, including alternate conformations of side chains and backbone segments, that better aligns with solution data and is in some cases more relevant to biological function (Fraser et al., 2009; Fraser et al., 2011; Fenwick et al., 2014; Keedy et al., 2015).
evidence: Cites multiple studies (Fraser et al., 2009; Fraser et al., 2011; Fenwick et al., 2014; Keedy et al., 2015) supporting this claim.

claim: RT crystallography can result in shifted binding poses for ligands compared to cryo temperature.
source: Past studies that focused on individual compounds or small sets of related/congeneric compounds have offered tantalizing hints, with RT resulting in shifted binding poses (Maeki et al., 2020; Bradford et al., 2021; Gildea et al., 2021; Milano et al., 2022), binding at a different site (Fischer et al., 2015), and even a change of crystal symmetry (Gildea et al., 2021).
evidence: Cites multiple studies showing shifted binding poses at RT.

claim: RT crystallography can result in ligands binding at a different site compared to cryo temperature.
source: Past studies that focused on individual compounds or small sets of related/congeneric compounds have offered tantalizing hints, with RT resulting in shifted binding poses (Maeki et al., 2020; Bradford et al., 2021; Gildea et al., 2021; Milano et al., 2022), binding at a different site (Fischer et al., 2015), and even a change of crystal symmetry (Gildea et al., 2021).
evidence: Cites Fischer et al., 2015 as evidence for binding at different sites.

claim: RT crystallography can result in a change of crystal symmetry.
source: Past studies that focused on individual compounds or small sets of related/congeneric compounds have offered tantalizing hints, with RT resulting in shifted binding poses (Maeki et al., 2020; Bradford et al., 2021; Gildea et al., 2021; Milano et al., 2022), binding at a different site (Fischer et al., 2015), and even a change of crystal symmetry (Gildea et al., 2021).
evidence: Cites Gildea et al., 2021 as evidence for crystal symmetry changes.

claim: Cryo temperature is reported to degrade the utility of crystal structures for computational docking and binding free energy calculations.
source: It also limits the potential of structure-based drug design (SBDD), given that cryo temperature is reported to degrade the utility of crystal structures for computational docking and binding free energy calculations (Bradford et al., 2021).
evidence: Cites Bradford et al., 2021 as evidence.

claim: A recent crystallographic fragment screen of the SARS-CoV-2 coronavirus's main protease (Mpro) provided dozens of starting points for crowd-sourcing the design of potent new small-molecule inhibitor candidates.
source: For example, a recent crystallographic fragment screen of the SARS-CoV-2 coronavirus's main protease (Mpro) (Douangamath et al., 2020) provided dozens of starting points for crowd-sourcing the design of potent new small-molecule inhibitor candidates (Achdout et al., 2022), complementing another crystallographic screen of Mpro using repurposed drug molecules (Günther et al., 2021).
evidence: Cites Douangamath et al., 2020 and Achdout et al., 2022 as supporting evidence.

claim: PTP1B is a highly validated therapeutic target for diabetes.
source: Previously, several authors of the current study performed a crystallographic fragment screen of the archetypal protein tyrosine phosphatase, PTP1B (also known as PTPN1) (Keedy et al., 2018), a highly validated therapeutic target for diabetes (Elchebly et al., 1999), cancer (Krishnan et al., 2014), and neurological disorders (Krishnan et al., 2015) that has also been deemed 'undruggable' (Zhang, 2017; Mullard, 2018).
evidence: Cites Elchebly et al., 1999 as evidence for diabetes target validation.

claim: PTP1B is a highly validated therapeutic target for cancer.
source: Previously, several authors of the current study performed a crystallographic fragment screen of the archetypal protein tyrosine phosphatase, PTP1B (also known as PTPN1) (Keedy et al., 2018), a highly validated therapeutic target for diabetes (Elchebly et al., 1999), cancer (Krishnan et al., 2014), and neurological disorders (Krishnan et al., 2015) that has also been deemed 'undruggable' (Zhang, 2017; Mullard, 2018).
evidence: Cites Krishnan et al., 2014 as evidence for cancer target validation.

claim: PTP1B is a highly validated therapeutic target for neurological disorders.
source: Previously, several authors of the current study performed a crystallographic fragment screen of the archetypal protein tyrosine phosphatase, PTP1B (also known as PTPN1) (Keedy et al., 2018), a highly validated therapeutic target for diabetes (Elchebly et al., 1999), cancer (Krishnan et al., 2014), and neurological disorders (Krishnan et al., 2015) that has also been deemed 'undruggable' (Zhang, 2017; Mullard, 2018).
evidence: Cites Krishnan et al., 2015 as evidence for neurological disorder target validation.

claim: PTP1B has been deemed 'undruggable'.
source: Previously, several authors of the current study performed a crystallographic fragment screen of the archetypal protein tyrosine phosphatase, PTP1B (also known as PTPN1) (Keedy et al., 2018), a highly validated therapeutic target for diabetes (Elchebly et al., 1999), cancer (Krishnan et al., 2014), and neurological disorders (Krishnan et al., 2015) that has also been deemed 'undruggable' (Zhang, 2017; Mullard, 2018).
evidence: Cites Zhang, 2017 and Mullard, 2018 as evidence for the 'undruggable' designation.

claim: A previous cryo fragment screen of PTP1B produced X-ray datasets for 1627 unique fragments, of which 110 were clearly resolved in electron density maps at 12 fragment-binding sites.
source: That fragment screen produced X-ray datasets for 1627 unique fragments, of which 110 were clearly resolved in electron density maps at 12 fragment-binding sites scattered across the surface of PTP1B.
evidence: Provides specific numbers from the previous study.

claim: One of the top three fragment-binding hotspots in PTP1B was previously validated with a non-covalent allosteric small-molecule inhibitor.
source: Of the top three fragment-binding 'hotspots', one was previously validated with a non-covalent allosteric small-molecule inhibitor (Wiesmann et al., 2004), and another was validated with a new covalent allosteric inhibitor inspired by the fragment hits (Keedy et al., 2018), thus highlighting fragment screening as a valuable tool for discovering allosteric footholds in proteins (Krojer et al., 2020).
evidence: Cites Wiesmann et al., 2004 as evidence for the non-covalent inhibitor validation.

claim: One of the top three fragment-binding hotspots in PTP1B was validated with a new covalent allosteric inhibitor inspired by the fragment hits.
source: Of the top three fragment-binding 'hotspots', one was previously validated with a non-covalent allosteric small-molecule inhibitor (Wiesmann et al., 2004), and another was validated with a new covalent allosteric inhibitor inspired by the fragment hits (Keedy et al., 2018), thus highlighting fragment screening as a valuable tool for discovering allosteric footholds in proteins (Krojer et al., 2020).
evidence: Cites Keedy et al., 2018 as evidence for the covalent inhibitor validation.

claim: Fragment screening is a valuable tool for discovering allosteric footholds in proteins.
source: Of the top three fragment-binding 'hotspots', one was previously validated with a non-covalent allosteric small-molecule inhibitor (Wiesmann et al., 2004), and another was validated with a new covalent allosteric inhibitor inspired by the fragment hits (Keedy et al., 2018), thus highlighting fragment screening as a valuable tool for discovering allosteric footholds in proteins (Krojer et al., 2020).
evidence: Cites Krojer et al., 2020 and provides examples from the PTP1B study.

claim: All previously reported crystallographic fragment screens were conducted at cryo temperature.
source: Importantly, however, all previously reported crystallographic fragment screens, including those mentioned above, were conducted at cryo temperature.
evidence: States this as a fact based on review of the literature.

claim: This study uses 143 unique, chemically diverse ligands, which is several-fold (4–5×) more than any previous RT crystallographic study.
source: Our work uses 143 unique, chemically diverse ligands which, to our knowledge, is several-fold (4–5×) more than any previous RT crystallographic study.
evidence: Provides specific number of ligands and comparison to previous studies.

claim: The two RT screens were performed with different diffraction data collection approaches, at different times, and with distinct but partially overlapping sets of fragments.
source: The two screens were performed with different diffraction data collection approaches, at different times, and with distinct but partially overlapping sets of fragments – so together they ensure that our overall conclusions are robust.
evidence: Describes the experimental design of the study.

claim: In both RT fragment screens, fewer fragments bind compared to cryo temperature.
source: In both RT fragment screens, we observe that fewer fragments bind, and on average more weakly (with lower occupancy).
evidence: States this as a result from the study.

claim: In both RT fragment screens, fragments bind on average more weakly (with lower occupancy) compared to cryo temperature.
source: In both RT fragment screens, we observe that fewer fragments bind, and on average more weakly (with lower occupancy).
evidence: States this as a result from the study.

claim: A fragment binds covalently to a key lysine in the allosteric 197 site.
source: Serendipitously, we also identify a fragment that binds covalently to a key lysine in the allosteric 197 site (Keedy et al., 2018), providing an intriguing new foothold for further allosteric inhibitor development.
evidence: States this as a result from the study.

claim: The fragment that binds covalently to Lys197 provides an intriguing new foothold for further allosteric inhibitor development.
source: Serendipitously, we also identify a fragment that binds covalently to a key lysine in the allosteric 197 site (Keedy et al., 2018), providing an intriguing new foothold for further allosteric inhibitor development.
evidence: Interprets the significance of the covalent binding result.

claim: The vast body of existing cryo-temperature protein-ligand structures may provide an incomplete picture.
source: Overall, this work suggests that the vast body of existing cryo-temperature protein-ligand structures may provide an incomplete picture, and highlights the potential of RT crystallography to help complete this picture by revealing distinct conformational modes of protein-ligand systems.
evidence: Interprets the implications of the study's findings.

claim: RT crystallography has the potential to reveal distinct conformational modes of protein-ligand systems.
source: Overall, this work suggests that the vast body of existing cryo-temperature protein-ligand structures may provide an incomplete picture, and highlights the potential of RT crystallography to help complete this picture by revealing distinct conformational modes of protein-ligand systems.
evidence: Interprets the implications of the study's findings.

claim: For the 1-xtal RT screen, the average resolution was 2.30 Å.
source: The data were high resolution for both RT screens (Figure 1): the average resolution was 2.30 Å for 1-xtal and 1.99 Å for in situ, as compared to 2.10 Å for the previous cryo screen (Keedy et al., 2018).
evidence: Provides specific resolution value and references Figure 1.

claim: For the in situ RT screen, the average resolution was 1.99 Å.
source: The data were high resolution for both RT screens (Figure 1): the average resolution was 2.30 Å for 1-xtal and 1.99 Å for in situ, as compared to 2.10 Å for the previous cryo screen (Keedy et al., 2018).
evidence: Provides specific resolution value and references Figure 1.

claim: For the previous cryo screen, the average resolution was 2.10 Å.
source: The data were high resolution for both RT screens (Figure 1): the average resolution was 2.30 Å for 1-xtal and 1.99 Å for in situ, as compared to 2.10 Å for the previous cryo screen (Keedy et al., 2018).
evidence: Provides specific resolution value and cites the previous study.

claim: The slightly lower resolution of the 1-xtal data may be due to some degree of radiation damage.
source: The slightly lower resolution of the 1-xtal data may be due to some degree of radiation damage, which was largely avoided by the in situ strategy (see Materials and methods).
evidence: Speculates on the cause of lower resolution.

claim: Radiation damage was largely avoided by the in situ strategy.
source: The slightly lower resolution of the 1-xtal data may be due to some degree of radiation damage, which was largely avoided by the in situ strategy (see Materials and methods).
evidence: States this as a fact about the experimental design.

claim: The results of the two RT screens are broadly very similar.
source: As outlined below, the results of the two screens are broadly very similar, and indeed identical for several fragments used in both screens (Figure 4—figure supplement 4), suggesting that radiation damage with the 1-xtal data was not a major factor in dictating our overall results.
evidence: Compares results between the two screens and references Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: The results are identical for several fragments used in both RT screens.
source: As outlined below, the results of the two screens are broadly very similar, and indeed identical for several fragments used in both screens (Figure 4—figure supplement 4), suggesting that radiation damage with the 1-xtal data was not a major factor in dictating our overall results.
evidence: States this as a result and references Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: Radiation damage with the 1-xtal data was not a major factor in dictating the overall results.
source: As outlined below, the results of the two screens are broadly very similar, and indeed identical for several fragments used in both screens (Figure 4—figure supplement 4), suggesting that radiation damage with the 1-xtal data was not a major factor in dictating our overall results.
evidence: Infers this from the similarity of results between the two screens.

claim: Visual inspection of all the 1-xtal RT hits did not show any signs of local radiation damage.
source: Additionally, a visual inspection of all the 1-xtal RT hits featured in this paper did not show any signs of local radiation damage (see Materials and methods).
evidence: States this as a result of visual inspection.

claim: The initial hit rates from PanDDA event maps were 12/38 (32%) for 1-xtal.
source: The initial hit rates from the event maps automatically generated by PanDDA were surprisingly low: 12/38 (32%) for 1-xtal and 7/48 (15%) for in situ.
evidence: Provides specific hit rate from the study.

claim: The initial hit rates from PanDDA event maps were 7/48 (15%) for in situ.
source: The initial hit rates from the event maps automatically generated by PanDDA were surprisingly low: 12/38 (32%) for 1-xtal and 7/48 (15%) for in situ.
evidence: Provides specific hit rate from the study.

claim: For cryo-non-hits, PanDDA revealed only two binding events, both for the same fragment in the same dataset.
source: Additionally, for cryo-non-hits, PanDDA revealed only two binding events; both were for the same fragment in the same dataset (vide infra).
evidence: Provides specific result from the study.

claim: Manual generation of RT event maps with the cryo value for 1-BDC identified five new binding events: three for the 1-xtal datasets and two for in situ datasets.
source: To identify hits that may have been missed by the automated PanDDA event identification algorithm, we manually generated RT event maps with the cryo value for 1-BDC, a quantity within PanDDA that is directly related to ligand-binding occupancy (Pearce et al., 2017a) (see Materials and methods). With this approach, we found five new binding events: three for the 1-xtal datasets and two for in situ datasets.
evidence: Provides specific result from the manual analysis and cites Pearce et al., 2017a for the 1-BDC definition.

claim: The final RT hit rate for cryo-hits was 15/38 (39%) for 1-xtal.
source: This brought the new totals to 15/38 (39%) for 1-xtal and 9/48 (19%) for in situ, still fairly low hit rates.
evidence: Provides specific hit rate after manual analysis.

claim: The final RT hit rate for cryo-hits was 9/48 (19%) for in situ before pre-clustering.
source: This brought the new totals to 15/38 (39%) for 1-xtal and 9/48 (19%) for in situ, still fairly low hit rates.
evidence: Provides specific hit rate after manual analysis.

claim: Pre-clustering of in situ wedges using cluster4x resulted in five additional hits that were not previously observed with the all-wedges datasets.
source: This pre-clustering protocol resulted in five additional hits that were not previously observed with the all-wedges datasets, bringing the total RT hit rate for cryo-hits up from 9/48 (19%) to 14/48 (29%) for in situ.
evidence: Provides specific result from the pre-clustering analysis.

claim: The final RT hit rate for cryo-hits was 14/48 (29%) for in situ after pre-clustering.
source: This pre-clustering protocol resulted in five additional hits that were not previously observed with the all-wedges datasets, bringing the total RT hit rate for cryo-hits up from 9/48 (19%) to 14/48 (29%) for in situ.
evidence: Provides specific hit rate after pre-clustering analysis.

claim: Many fragments have lower occupancy at RT than at cryo.
source: Many fragments have lower occupancy at RT than at cryo (Figure 2).
evidence: States this as a result and references Figure 2.

claim: The trend of lower occupancy at RT holds for cryo-hits that bind to the cryo site at RT either with the same pose or with a new pose.
source: This trend holds for cryo-hits that bind to the cryo site at RT either with the same pose (blue points in Figure 2) or with a new pose (orange points in Figure 2) (see Table 2).
evidence: States this as a result and references Figure 2 and Table 2.

claim: Between the two RT screens, there are 29 new RT events with small-molecule fragments.
source: Between our two RT screens, we have 15+14 = 29 new RT events with small-molecule fragments.
evidence: Provides specific count of RT events.

claim: RT fragment hits are bound at sites distributed throughout PTP1B, including at least one at the active site and at all three allosteric sites previously highlighted by the cryo screen.
source: The RT fragment hits are bound at sites distributed throughout PTP1B, including at least one at the active site and at all three allosteric sites previously highlighted by the cryo screen (Keedy et al., 2018): the 197 site, BB site, and L16 site (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: States this as a result and references Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and the previous study.

claim: Many of the key binding sites have RT hits in both the 1-xtal and in situ screens.
source: Many of these sites have RT hits in both the 1-xtal and in situ screens (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), confirming the success of both screens.
evidence: States this as a result and references Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: In all four key sites (active site, 197 site, BB site, L16 site), one or more fragments bind differently from cryo.
source: Notably, in all of these four key sites, one or more fragments bind differently from cryo – either binding with a new pose at RT or binding to this site only at RT and not cryo (Figure 3).
evidence: States this as a result and references Figure 3.

claim: Of the cryo-hits that also bind at RT, most do so with a similar pose: 9 cases for 1-xtal and 7 for in situ.
source: Of the cryo-hits that also bind at RT, most do so with a similar pose (Figure 4, Table 2): 9 cases for 1-xtal (Figure 4—figure supplement 1) and 7 for in situ (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Provides specific counts and references figures and table.

claim: Of the three fragments with binding events in both the 1-xtal and in situ screens, all three bind similarly in both RT screens.
source: Notably, of the three fragments with binding events in both the 1-xtal and in situ screens, all three bind similarly in both RT screens (Figure 4—figure supplement 4), suggesting the RT results are reproducible and reliable.
evidence: States this as a result and references Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: The RT results are reproducible and reliable.
source: Notably, of the three fragments with binding events in both the 1-xtal and in situ screens, all three bind similarly in both RT screens (Figure 4—figure supplement 4), suggesting the RT results are reproducible and reliable.
evidence: Infers this from the consistency of results between the two screens.

claim: In some cases, clear event map density is present for a water at RT but not at cryo.
source: In a few examples, clear event map density is present for a water at RT but not at cryo (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 5A–B) or vice versa (Figure 4—figure supplement 5C), even when varying event map contour levels.
evidence: States this as a result and references specific figures.

claim: In some cases, clear event map density is present for a water at cryo but not at RT.
source: In a few examples, clear event map density is present for a water at RT but not at cryo (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 5A–B) or vice versa (Figure 4—figure supplement 5C), even when varying event map contour levels.
evidence: States this as a result and references specific figures.

claim: Even when ligand binding is similar, the solvation layer around the ligand can change at cryo vs. RT.
source: Therefore, even when ligand binding is similar, the solvation layer around the ligand can change at cryo vs. RT.
evidence: Infers this from the observed differences in water molecule positions.

claim: A fragment binds in the allosteric L16 site with the central ring in the same position at RT vs. cryo, but with substantially different positions for the two substituent groups.
source: In one striking example, the fragment binds with the central ring in the same position at RT vs. cryo, but with substantially different positions for the two substituent groups (Figure 5).
evidence: States this as a result and references Figure 5.

claim: The RT density for the fragment in the L16 site is incompatible with the cryo model, and vice versa.
source: The in-plane chlorine and out-of-plane methylamine group are clearly defined in the respective event maps: the RT density is incompatible with the cryo model, and vice versa.
evidence: States this as a result from visual inspection of the maps.

claim: The allosteric L16 site was first reported alongside the original cryo fragment screen for PTP1B and highlighted as a promising target for small-molecule allosteric inhibitor development.
source: Notably, this fragment binds in the allosteric L16 site (Figure 3), which was first reported alongside the original cryo fragment screen for PTP1B and highlighted as a promising target for small-molecule allosteric inhibitor development (Keedy et al., 2018).
evidence: Cites Keedy et al., 2018 as the source of this information.

claim: A fragment exhibits alternate ligand conformations that coexist in the same site, but only at one temperature.
source: Another example features alternate ligand conformations that coexist in the same site, but only at one temperature.
evidence: States this as a result from the study.

claim: The RT event map for a specific fragment suggests a pose with the carbonyl pointed toward Arg238.
source: The RT event map suggests a pose with the carbonyl pointed one direction, toward Arg238 (Figure 6A).
evidence: States this as a result and references Figure 6A.

claim: At cryo, a specific fragment was modeled with the carbonyl rotated by a 180° flip, enabling a water-bridged H-bond.
source: However, at cryo, this fragment was previously modeled with the carbonyl rotated by a 180° flip, enabling a water-bridged H-bond (Figure 6B).
evidence: States this as a result and references Figure 6B.

claim: The RT event map for a specific fragment has weak evidence at best for the flipped cryo conformation.
source: The RT event map has weak evidence at best for the flipped cryo conformation (Figure 6A).
evidence: States this as a result and references Figure 6A.

claim: The cryo event map for a specific fragment has significant evidence for both conformations.
source: By contrast, the cryo event map has significant evidence for both conformations (Figure 6B).
evidence: States this as a result and references Figure 6B.

claim: Ligand conformational heterogeneity can be temperature-dependent.
source: This observation is akin to other examples in which a ligand exhibits conformational heterogeneity in a single X-ray dataset (van Zundert et al., 2018). Here, however, the ligand conformational heterogeneity is temperature-dependent, enabling cross-pollination of conformations across temperatures to improve modeling (Keedy, 2019; Bradford et al., 2021).
evidence: Infers this from the observed differences and cites related work.

claim: For two related fragments, the RT event density shows the fragment binds with its longer substituent well ordered and pointed underneath the active-site WPD loop, which closes over the fragment.
source: In each of these two related examples, the RT event density is clear that the fragment binds with its longer substituent well ordered and pointed underneath the active-site WPD loop, which closes over the fragment (Figure 7A and B, left panels).
evidence: States this as a result and references Figure 7A and B.

claim: At cryo, for two related fragments, the loop still closes over the fragment, and the core of the fragment is in a similar location, but the longer substituent seems to protrude toward solution.
source: At cryo, the loop still closes over the fragment, and the core of the fragment is in a similar location. However, the cryo event density is inconsistent with the RT pose – instead, the longer substituent seems to protrude toward solution (Figure 7A and B, right panels).
evidence: States this as a result and references Figure 7A and B.

claim: For one of two related fragments, a new ordered water molecule at cryo displaces the RT ligand pose.
source: For one of these fragments, a new ordered water molecule at cryo displaces the RT ligand pose (Figure 7B).
evidence: States this as a result and references Figure 7B.

claim: Temperature can modulate what protein site a ligand binds to.
source: Beyond just differences within the same binding site, temperature can also modulate ligand binding more dramatically, even altering what protein site the ligand binds to.
evidence: States this as a general conclusion from the study.

claim: A fragment binds to the allosteric BB site at cryo, but there is no event density at RT; instead, there is strong fragment-binding event density at a different site nearly 40 Å away.
source: In a first example, the fragment binds to the allosteric BB site (Wiesmann et al., 2004; Keedy et al., 2018) at cryo (Figure 8A and C), but there is no event density at RT. Instead, there is strong fragment-binding event density at a different site nearly 40 Å away (Figure 8A and B).
evidence: States this as a result and references Figure 8A, B, and C, and cites previous work.

claim: The RT event density for a fragment that switches sites supports subtle protein shifts in the new binding site to accommodate the new fragment-binding event.
source: The RT event density supports subtle protein shifts in the new binding site to accommodate the new fragment-binding event (Figure 8B).
evidence: States this as a result and references Figure 8B.

claim: In the cryo-binding site for a fragment that switches sites at RT, the RT protein conformation would clash with the cryo pose, disallowing binding at RT.
source: By contrast, in the cryo-binding site, the RT protein conformation would clash with the cryo pose, disallowing binding at RT.
evidence: Infers this from the structural analysis.

claim: At cryo, a fragment binds with an artifactual stacking arrangement involving three copies of the fragment, but at RT there is no event density for this stacking.
source: In additional examples, elevated temperature dissipates what seem to be cryo-binding artifacts. In the first such example, at cryo the fragment binds with an artifactual stacking arrangement involving three copies of the fragment (Figure 8D and E), but at RT there is no event density (automated or custom) for this stacking.
evidence: States this as a result and references Figure 8D and E.

claim: Temperature can modulate protein-ligand energy landscapes significantly, in some cases by disfavoring enthalpically favorable stacking at higher temperature.
source: This result suggests that temperature can modulate protein-ligand energy landscapes significantly, in this case by disfavoring enthalpically favorable stacking at higher temperature.
evidence: Infers this from the observed disappearance of stacking at RT.

claim: At RT, new event density for a fragment appears at a distal site that is over 45 Å away from the cryo site.
source: Moreover, at RT, new event density for a single copy of this fragment appears at a distal site (Figure 8F) that is over 45 Å away from the cryo site (Figure 8D).
evidence: States this as a result and references Figure 8D and F.

claim: Cryo event density at a new RT-binding site was too weak to justify modeling a bound fragment in the previous cryo screen.
source: Cryo event density at the new site was too weak to justify modeling a bound fragment (Keedy et al., 2018).
evidence: Cites the previous study as the source of this information.

claim: For one fragment, the cryo-binding site is unique to cryo and the RT-binding site is unique to RT.
source: Thus, the cryo-binding site is unique to cryo and the RT-binding site is unique to RT.
evidence: Infers this from the observed binding patterns.

claim: One fragment binds at RT to a new site that was not previously thought to bind any fragments at cryo.
source: In fact, this is the only case in which a fragment binds at RT to a new site that was not previously thought to bind any fragments at cryo (although later computational reanalysis did discover one previously undetected adjacent cryo-hit in this area; Ginn, 2020).
evidence: States this as a result and cites Ginn, 2020 for the later reanalysis.

claim: A Tris buffer molecule binds in the same location as a new RT fragment-binding site in another published structure (PDB ID 4y14).
source: A Tris buffer molecule also fortuitously binds in the same location in another published structure (PDB ID 4y14), although it is held in place by a distinct crystal contact due to that structure's space group.
evidence: Cites PDB ID 4y14 as evidence.

claim: A fragment previously bound at cryo with an artifactual stacking arrangement involving two copies of the fragment; at RT, one copy remains bound.
source: In a related but distinct case, a fragment previously bound at cryo with a seemingly similar artifactual stacking arrangement, this time involving two copies of the fragment (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A). However, at RT the entire stack does not disappear – instead, one copy remains bound (Figure 8—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: States this as a result and references Figure 8—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: At cryo, for a fragment with a two-copy stack, one copy was slightly more ordered than the other, based on event map strength.
source: At cryo, this latter copy was slightly more ordered than the other, based on event map strength.
evidence: States this as a result from the cryo data.

claim: Elevated temperature is sufficient to displace the more weakly bound copy of a fragment, but not the more tightly bound one.
source: Thus, elevated temperature is sufficient to displace the more weakly bound copy, but not the more tightly bound one.
evidence: Infers this from the observed binding patterns at RT vs. cryo.

claim: A fragment previously bound at three distal sites at cryo; at RT the fragment binds to only one of the cryo sites, in a nearly identical pose.
source: In a final, somewhat more complicated example, a fragment previously bound at three distal sites at cryo. At RT the fragment binds to only one of the cryo sites, in a nearly identical pose.
evidence: States this as a result from the study.

claim: In the other cryo sites for a fragment that bound at three sites at cryo, RT-binding events were not readily detected, either automatically by PanDDA or in RT event maps calculated at the cryo events' 1-BDC values.
source: In the other cryo sites, RT-binding events were not readily detected, either automatically by PanDDA or in RT event maps calculated at the cryo events' 1-BDC values.
evidence: States this as a result from the analysis.

claim: At RT, a fragment that bound at three sites at cryo now binds to an additional new site that is over 40 Å away from any of the three cryo sites.
source: More strikingly, at RT the fragment now binds to an additional new site (Figure 8—figure supplement 2A and B) that is over 40 Å away from any of the three cryo sites (Figure 8—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: States this as a result and references Figure 8—figure supplement 2A, B, and C.

claim: Although fragment binding was clear in cryo event maps at three cryo sites, cryo density was unconvincing at a new RT site; therefore, no binding event was detectable at this new site at cryo.
source: Although fragment binding was clear in cryo event maps at the three cryo sites, cryo density was unconvincing at the RT site; therefore, no binding event was detectable at this new site at cryo.
evidence: States this as a result from the analysis.

claim: One fragment binds only in RT datasets and in an unexpected fashion.
source: In addition to the fragments that switch binding sites at RT as detailed above, one fragment binds only in our RT datasets – and in an unexpected fashion.
evidence: States this as a result from the study.

claim: In RT event maps, strong event density is observed at/near both the allosteric 197 and L16 sites, contiguous with the side chains of nearby lysine residues, consistent with covalent binding by an isatin-based fragment.
source: In RT event maps, we observe strong event density at/near both the allosteric 197 and L16 sites (Keedy et al., 2018). Surprisingly, at each site, the event density is contiguous with the side chains of a nearby lysine residue (Figure 9), consistent with covalent binding by the isatin-based fragment.
evidence: States this as a result and references Figure 9 and the previous study.

claim: At the allosteric L16 site, a fragment binds covalently to Lys237 (part of Loop 16), adjacent to the L16 pocket itself, nearer to the allosteric BB site.
source: First, at the allosteric L16 site, the fragment binds covalently to Lys237 (part of the eponymous Loop 16) – although it binds adjacent to the L16 pocket itself, nearer to the allosteric BB site (Figure 9C).
evidence: States this as a result and references Figure 9C.

claim: At the allosteric 197 site, a fragment binds covalently to Lys197 with a pose that is strikingly similar to that of a covalent allosteric inhibitor tethered to a K197C mutant.
source: Second, at the allosteric 197 site site, the fragment binds covalently to Lys197 with a pose that is strikingly similar to that of a covalent allosteric inhibitor tethered to a K197C mutant (Keedy et al., 2018; Figure 9A).
evidence: States this as a result and references Figure 9A and the previous study.

claim: The distal active-site P loop and substrate-binding loop adopt new conformations that are similar to those observed when the catalytic Cys215 is oxidized.
source: The distal active-site P loop and substrate-binding loop adopt new conformations that are similar to those observed when the catalytic Cys215 is oxidized (van Montfort et al., 2003), although it is unclear whether Cys215 is oxidized in our RT event map.
evidence: States this as a result and cites van Montfort et al., 2003.

claim: It is unclear whether Cys215 is oxidized in the RT event map for the covalently bound fragment.
source: The distal active-site P loop and substrate-binding loop adopt new conformations that are similar to those observed when the catalytic Cys215 is oxidized (van Montfort et al., 2003), although it is unclear whether Cys215 is oxidized in our RT event map.
evidence: States uncertainty about the oxidation state.

claim: The new loop conformations observed with the covalently bound fragment were not observed with the K197C-tethered allosteric inhibitor.
source: These conformations were not observed with the K197C-tethered allosteric inhibitor (Figure 9—figure supplement 1).
evidence: States this as a result and references Figure 9—figure supplement 1.

claim: The covalently binding fragment is a cryo-non-hit, meaning it demonstrably did not bind at cryo despite a high-resolution cryo dataset (1.89 Å, y1159).
source: This fragment is a cryo-non-hit, meaning it demonstrably did not bind at cryo despite a high-resolution cryo dataset (1.89 Å, y1159).
evidence: States this as a fact from the study.

claim: The covalently binding fragment is the only cryo-non-hit to bind in either RT screen.
source: Indeed, it is the only cryo-non-hit to bind in either RT screen.
evidence: States this as a fact from the study.

claim: The covalently binding cryo-non-hit was chemically dissimilar to all previous cryo-hits: the most similar cryo-hit has a low Tanimoto score relative to this RT fragment (0.36, y1703) and does not bind near the RT sites.
source: This cryo-non-hit was chemically dissimilar to all previous cryo-hits: the most similar cryo-hit has a low Tanimoto score relative to this RT fragment (0.36, y1703) and does not bind near the RT sites.
evidence: Provides specific Tanimoto score as evidence.

claim: It is possible that the crystal for the cryo dataset of the covalently binding fragment was insufficiently soaked with this compound.
source: It is possible that the crystal for the cryo dataset was insufficiently soaked with this compound, or that the new RT-binding events seen here are due to additional chemical changes to the compound in DMSO solvent over time that altered its reactivity toward lysines.
evidence: Speculates on possible reasons for the lack of cryo binding.

claim: It is possible that the new RT-binding events for the covalently binding fragment are due to additional chemical changes to the compound in DMSO solvent over time that altered its reactivity toward lysines.
source: It is possible that the crystal for the cryo dataset was insufficiently soaked with this compound, or that the new RT-binding events seen here are due to additional chemical changes to the compound in DMSO solvent over time that altered its reactivity toward lysines.
evidence: Speculates on possible reasons for the RT binding.

claim: The covalently binding fragment does not inhibit PTP1B with an in vitro activity assay.
source: As expected for fragments due to their weak binding affinities, this molecule does not inhibit PTP1B with an in vitro activity assay (Keedy et al., 2018) (data not shown).
evidence: States this as a result from an activity assay.

claim: Optimized versions of the covalently binding fragment, particularly driven by fragment linking of the K197C-targeted compound and this new fragment, could yield potent allosteric inhibitors for wildtype (WT) PTP1B, without need for mutation to a cysteine.
source: However, our observations here raise the hope that optimized versions of this compound, particularly driven by fragment linking of the K197C-targeted compound and this new fragment (Figure 9A), could yield potent allosteric inhibitors for wildtype (WT) PTP1B, without need for mutation to a cysteine.
evidence: Speculates on the potential for future drug development based on the results.

claim: Temperature affects not only fragment binding to the protein but also the protein's conformational response to fragment binding.
source: Temperature does not only affect fragment binding to the protein – it can also affect the protein's conformational response to fragment binding.
evidence: States this as a general conclusion from the study.

claim: Protein conformational responses to fragment binding are preferentially localized to the key allosteric sites that were identified in a previous study as being inherently linked to the active site.
source: With both screens, we observe protein conformational responses that are preferentially localized to the key allosteric sites that were identified in our previous study as being inherently linked to the active site (Keedy et al., 2018).
evidence: States this as a result and cites the previous study.

claim: At cryo, fragments in the L16 site that intercalate below the α6 helix push it further in the direction of α7, the BB site, and the rest of the allosteric network.
source: At cryo, fragments in this site that intercalate below the α6 helix push it further in the direction of α7, the BB site, and the rest of the allosteric network (Keedy et al., 2018).
evidence: Cites the previous study as the source of this information.

claim: At RT, structures with two fragments in the L16 site show that they affect the position of α6 similarly at RT vs. cryo.
source: At RT, structures with two of these fragments (Figure 4—figure supplement 2G, Figure 5) show that they affect the position of α6 similarly at RT vs. cryo (Figure 10—video 1); perhaps surprisingly, this remains true despite one fragment exhibiting a 180° pose flip (Figure 5).
evidence: States this as a result and references specific figures.

claim: The effect on α6 position remains similar at RT vs. cryo despite one fragment exhibiting a 180° pose flip.
source: At RT, structures with two of these fragments (Figure 4—figure supplement 2G, Figure 5) show that they affect the position of α6 similarly at RT vs. cryo (Figure 10—video 1); perhaps surprisingly, this remains true despite one fragment exhibiting a 180° pose flip (Figure 5).
evidence: States this as a result.

claim: In the allosteric BB site, although a fragment binds in the same pose at RT and cryo, an entire additional helical turn of α6 is ordered at RT.
source: However, in the nearby allosteric BB site (Wiesmann et al., 2004), the α6 helix is differentially ordered upon binding of a fragment at RT vs. cryo (Figure 10). Although the fragment binds in the same pose at RT and cryo, an entire additional helical turn of α6 is ordered at RT.
evidence: States this as a result and references Figure 10 and cites Wiesmann et al., 2004.

claim: Temperature can modulate not only the positions of protein structural elements during ligand binding, but also their relative order vs. disorder.
source: This example illustrates that temperature can modulate not only the positions of protein structural elements during ligand binding, but also their relative order vs. disorder.
evidence: Infers this from the observed differences in α6 helix ordering.

claim: A fragment binds in the 197 site with a similar pose at cryo and RT.
source: Elsewhere on the contiguous allosteric back face of PTP1B, in the 197 site (Keedy et al., 2018), a fragment binds with a similar pose at cryo and RT (Figure 11, Figure 11—figure supplement 1).
evidence: States this as a result and references Figure 11 and Figure 11—figure supplement 1.

claim: When a fragment binds in the 197 site at cryo, the protein globally remains in its default open state.
source: When this fragment binds at cryo, the protein globally remains in its default open state (Figure 11).
evidence: States this as a result and references Figure 11.

claim: When a fragment binds in the 197 site at RT, the allosteric L16 site closes, and the active-site WPD loop partially closes.
source: However, at RT, the allosteric L16 site closes, and the active-site WPD loop partially closes (Figure 11).
evidence: States this as a result and references Figure 11.

claim: A fragment that binds in the 197 site binds in the same position as a previously reported covalently tethered allosteric inhibitor.
source: Notably, this fragment binds in the same position as a previously reported covalently tethered allosteric inhibitor (Keedy et al., 2018; Figure 11—figure supplement 2; see also Figure 9).
evidence: States this as a result and references Figure 11—figure supplement 2 and Figure 9, and cites the previous study.

claim: RT allows for distinct protein conformational redistributions in response to fragment binding in allosteric sites.
source: Thus, RT allows for distinct protein conformational redistributions in response to fragment binding in allosteric sites.
evidence: Infers this from the observed conformational changes at RT.

claim: Only 29–39% of the fragments that previously bound at cryo temperature also bound at RT.
source: Although only 29–39% of the fragments that previously bound at cryo temperature (Keedy et al., 2018) also bound here at RT, several lines of evidence suggest this is predominantly due to the difference in data collection temperature, as opposed to, for example, variability in experimental steps.
evidence: Provides specific percentages from the study.

claim: The difference in binding rates between cryo and RT is predominantly due to the difference in data collection temperature, as opposed to variability in experimental steps.
source: Although only 29–39% of the fragments that previously bound at cryo temperature (Keedy et al., 2018) also bound here at RT, several lines of evidence suggest this is predominantly due to the difference in data collection temperature, as opposed to, for example, variability in experimental steps.
evidence: Infers this from multiple lines of evidence presented in the discussion.

claim: The RT hit rates for cryo-hits were similar for the two RT screens, which were performed with different techniques by largely different sets of people at different times.
source: First, the RT hit rates for cryo-hits were similar for our two RT screens, which were performed with different techniques (single-crystal and in situ) by largely different sets of people at different times.
evidence: States this as evidence for the temperature-dependent effect.

claim: Log files from the acoustic droplet ejection instrument used for soaking were monitored and any crystals that may not have been soaked correctly were excluded.
source: Second, we monitored log files from the acoustic droplet ejection instrument used for soaking (Collins et al., 2017) and excluded any crystals that may not have been soaked correctly.
evidence: States this as evidence for proper experimental procedure and cites Collins et al., 2017.

claim: In multiple RT datasets, a cryo-hit fragment demonstrably no longer binds at the original site but does bind at a different site, confirming the crystals were soaked correctly.
source: Third, in multiple RT datasets, a cryo-hit fragment demonstrably no longer binds at the original site but does bind at a different site (Figure 8), confirming the crystals were soaked correctly.
evidence: States this as evidence for proper experimental procedure and references Figure 8.

claim: Even when cryo-hit fragments are observed in RT electron density event maps, there is a trend of lower occupancies at RT.
source: Fourth, even when cryo-hit fragments are observed in RT electron density event maps, we observe a trend of lower occupancies at RT (Figure 2).
evidence: States this as evidence for the temperature-dependent effect and references Figure 2.

claim: The large temperature difference between cryo and RT (>178 K) underlies the observed changes in binding.
source: We conclude that the large temperature difference between cryo and RT (>178 K) underlies the observed changes in binding.
evidence: Concludes this based on the evidence presented.

claim: In a recent study, 0 of 9 cryo-hit ligands were seen to bind at RT.
source: This is in accord with recent studies in which only 0 of 9 (Guven et al., 2021) and 5 of 30 (Gildea et al., 2021) cryo-hit ligands were seen to bind at RT, and in which lower occupancies were seen at RT than at cryo for <10 ligands (Bradford et al., 2021).
evidence: Cites Guven et al., 2021 as supporting evidence.

claim: In a recent study, 5 of 30 cryo-hit ligands were seen to bind at RT.
source: This is in accord with recent studies in which only 0 of 9 (Guven et al., 2021) and 5 of 30 (Gildea et al., 2021) cryo-hit ligands were seen to bind at RT, and in which lower occupancies were seen at RT than at cryo for <10 ligands (Bradford et al., 2021).
evidence: Cites Gildea et al., 2021 as supporting evidence.

claim: In a recent study, lower occupancies were seen at RT than at cryo for <10 ligands.
source: This is in accord with recent studies in which only 0 of 9 (Guven et al., 2021) and 5 of 30 (Gildea et al., 2021) cryo-hit ligands were seen to bind at RT, and in which lower occupancies were seen at RT than at cryo for <10 ligands (Bradford et al., 2021).
evidence: Cites Bradford et al., 2021 as supporting evidence.

claim: After crystal soaking at ambient temperature, all cryo-hit fragments are initially bound, but in many cases only loosely, with high B-factors that render them invisible from RT diffraction data.
source: How does higher diffraction temperature cause such significant changes in protein-ligand binding? We speculate that after crystal soaking (which occurs at ambient temperature), all cryo-hit fragments are initially bound, but in many cases only loosely, with high B-factors that render them invisible from RT diffraction data.
evidence: Speculates on the mechanism underlying the temperature effect.

claim: During cryocooling, the ligand B-factors drop rapidly on a faster timescale than overall crystal cooling, with many becoming sufficiently well ordered to be observable in cryo density.
source: During cryocooling, the ligand B-factors (i.e. temperature factors) then drop rapidly on a faster timescale than overall crystal cooling (Halle, 2004), with many becoming sufficiently well ordered to be observable in cryo density (at least with PanDDA).
evidence: Speculates on the mechanism and cites Halle, 2004 for the B-factor behavior.

claim: Fragments that bind at both cryo and RT, but with a different pose or binding site, have similar molecular weights and numbers of rotatable bonds, yet are more hydrophobic and have more interactions with the binding site.
source: Relatedly, it is unclear why some fragments bind at both cryo and RT, but with a different pose or binding site: they have similar molecular weights and numbers of rotatable bonds, yet are more hydrophobic and have more interactions with the binding site (Table 2—source data 2).
evidence: States this as a result from the analysis and references Table 2—source data 2.

claim: Additional experiments are planned using mechanically controlled variable cryocooling rate and variable crystal size to more deeply interrogate the complex relationship between temperature, cooling kinetics, and protein-ligand conformational ensembles.
source: To more deeply interrogate the complex relationship between temperature, cooling kinetics, and protein-ligand conformational ensembles, additional experiments are planned using mechanically controlled variable cryocooling rate (Warkentin et al., 2006) and variable crystal size.
evidence: States this as a plan for future work and cites Warkentin et al., 2006.

claim: Future studies can explore the degree to which the conclusions drawn here for small-molecule fragments can be extrapolated to larger, drug-sized ligands.
source: Future studies can also explore the degree to which the conclusions drawn here for small-molecule fragments can be extrapolated to larger, drug-sized ligands.
evidence: States this as a direction for future work.

claim: Cryo crystal structures of proteins have greater inherent variability than do RT structures, presumably due to idiosyncratic crystal cryocooling kinetics.
source: Previous work has shown that cryo crystal structures of proteins have greater inherent variability than do RT structures, presumably due to idiosyncratic crystal cryocooling kinetics (Keedy et al., 2014).
evidence: Cites Keedy et al., 2014 as supporting evidence.

claim: No work has examined replicates of many fragment-soaked cryo crystal structures to establish the impact of crystal variability on details of fragment binding such as pose.
source: However, despite growing interest in crystallographic fragment screening, no work has examined replicates of many fragment-soaked cryo crystal structures to establish the impact of crystal variability on details of fragment binding such as pose.
evidence: States this as a gap in the literature.

claim: In a study using fragment screens with two different crystal forms of the same protein, most fragments did not bind in both crystal forms, and of those that did, only two of five bound in the same site with the same pose.
source: One study using fragment screens with two different crystal forms of the same protein showed that most fragments did not bind in both crystal forms, and of those that did, only two of five bound in the same site with the same pose (Schuller et al., 2021); however, this is a different situation from repeats of the same fragment in the same crystal form.
evidence: Cites Schuller et al., 2021 as evidence.

claim: Crystallographically refined occupancies of ligands approach saturation at ~15 min of soaking time.
source: Another study showed that crystallographically refined occupancies of ligands approach saturation at ~15 min of soaking time (Cole et al., 2014) however, our soaking times were many hours (Keedy et al., 2018), so this should not be a significant source of variability in our datasets.
evidence: Cites Cole et al., 2014 and Keedy et al., 2018 as evidence.

claim: The PanDDA algorithm seeks to overcome dataset variability by averaging to establish a reliable ground state density estimate for the purposes of identifying hits.
source: The PanDDA algorithm seeks to overcome (typically cryo) dataset variability by averaging to establish a reliable ground state density estimate for the purposes of identifying hits, yet individual hits may still have idiosyncratic features.
evidence: Describes the function of the PanDDA algorithm.

claim: Future studies focused on fragment (and larger ligand) reproducibility in terms of binding occupancy, site, and pose at cryo temperature would be useful contributions to the field.
source: Overall, future studies focused on fragment (and larger ligand) reproducibility in terms of binding occupancy, site, and pose at cryo temperature would be useful contributions to the field.
evidence: States this as a recommendation for future work.

claim: One case involves essentially complete closing of the allosteric L16 site, but only partial closing (~50%) of the active-site WPD loop, in contrast to the previous paradigm in which the WPD loop and allosteric sites are precisely conformationally coupled.
source: One case involves essentially complete closing of the allosteric L16 site, but only partial closing (~50%) of the active-site WPD loop (Figure 11) – in contrast to the previous paradigm in which the WPD loop and allosteric sites are precisely conformationally coupled (Keedy et al., 2018).
evidence: States this as a result and references Figure 11 and cites the previous study.

claim: Similar (de)coupling of the WPD loop and allosteric sites was also seen recently with serial synchrotron crystallography of apo PTP1B.
source: Similar (de)coupling was also seen recently with serial synchrotron crystallography of apo PTP1B (Sharma et al., 2023).
evidence: Cites Sharma et al., 2023 as supporting evidence.

claim: RT crystallography can add important nuance to our understanding of allosteric mechanisms in PTPs and likely other proteins.
source: Thus, RT crystallography can add important nuance to our understanding of allosteric mechanisms in PTPs (Choy et al., 2017; Cui et al., 2017; Hjortness et al., 2018) and likely other proteins.
evidence: Infers this from the results and cites related work on PTPs.

claim: New conformations for fragments on both sides of Loop 16 of the allosteric L16 site offer unique footholds for structure-based inhibitor design of allosteric inhibitors.
source: First, we observe new conformations for fragments on both sides of Loop 16 of the allosteric L16 site (Figure 5, Figure 6), offering unique footholds for structure-based inhibitor design of allosteric inhibitors.
evidence: Infers this from the observed new conformations and references Figure 5 and Figure 6.

claim: Local ligand heterogeneity in the L16 site, combined with the malleability of the adjacent α6 helix and varying levels of apparent coupling between the L16 and active sites, argue for additional studies to decipher how different ligands in this region may selectively perturb the conformations of remote sites to allosterically control PTP1B function.
source: This local ligand heterogeneity, combined with the malleability of the adjacent α6 helix (Figure 10, Figure 10—video 1) and varying levels of apparent coupling between the L16 and active sites (Figure 11), argue for additional studies to decipher how different ligands in this region may selectively perturb the conformations of remote sites to allosterically control PTP1B function.
evidence: Infers this from the results and references Figure 10, Figure 10—video 1, and Figure 11.

claim: One new RT fragment-binding site was not previously shown to bind any fragments at cryo, thus offering a new ligand-binding foothold.
source: Second, one new RT fragment-binding site reported here was not previously shown to bind any fragments at cryo (Keedy et al., 2018) although additional clustering did identify one adjacent cryo-hit (Ginn, 2020), thus offering a new ligand-binding foothold.
evidence: States this as a result and cites the previous study and Ginn, 2020.

claim: The corresponding site to a new RT fragment-binding site in the paralog SHP2 has been successfully targeted with small-molecule allosteric inhibitors that stabilize a regulatory domain interface in the auto-inhibited state.
source: Coincidentally, the corresponding site in the paralog SHP2 has been successfully targeted with small-molecule allosteric inhibitors that stabilize a regulatory domain interface in the auto-inhibited state (Chen et al., 2016; LaRochelle et al., 2018).
evidence: Cites Chen et al., 2016 and LaRochelle et al., 2018 as evidence.

claim: Although PTP1B lacks the additional regulatory domain present in SHP2, it may nonetheless harbor latent allosteric capabilities that stem from the region corresponding to the SHP2 allosteric site within the catalytic domain.
source: Although PTP1B lacks this additional regulatory domain, our data suggest future studies to explore whether it may nonetheless harbor latent allosteric capabilities that stem from this region within the catalytic domain.
evidence: Speculates on the potential for allosteric regulation based on the results.

claim: The observation of a fragment covalently bound to Lys197 of the allosteric 197 site opens new doors to design a covalent allosteric inhibitor targeting WT PTP1B.
source: Third, we observe a fragment covalently bound to Lys197 of the allosteric 197 site, with a similar pose as our previously reported allosteric inhibitor that was covalently tethered to an engineered K197C mutant (Keedy et al., 2018; Figure 9). This unexpected result opens new doors to design a covalent allosteric inhibitor targeting WT PTP1B, inspired by other success stories of progressing covalent fragment hits (Miller et al., 2013; Resnick et al., 2019).
evidence: Infers this from the result and cites related work on covalent inhibitors.

claim: The potential of targeting the allosteric 197 site of PTP1B is further reinforced by the finding that fragment binding in this site can elicit allosteric conformational responses at RT that were masked at cryo.
source: The potential of targeting the allosteric 197 site of PTP1B is further reinforced by our new finding that fragment binding in this site (Figure 11—figure supplement 1) can elicit allosteric conformational responses at RT that were masked at cryo (Figure 11).
evidence: Infers this from the results and references Figure 11 and Figure 11—figure supplement 1.

claim: RT fragments are bound in all three previously reported surface allosteric sites in the PTP1B catalytic domain: the BB site, the 197 site, and the L16 site.
source: Altogether, we observe RT fragments bound in a variety of sites in PTP1B with potential for enabling downstream allosteric drug design. We see fragments bound in all three previously reported surface allosteric sites in the PTP1B catalytic domain: the BB site (Wiesmann et al., 2004), the 197 site (Keedy et al., 2018), and the L16 site (Keedy et al., 2018).
evidence: States this as a result and cites the relevant studies.

claim: The BB site is also thought to be near a secondary binding site for a second class of allosteric inhibitors for PTP1B, for example, MSI-1436, which primarily targets a different site in the disordered C-terminus.
source: The BB site is also thought to be near a secondary binding site for a second class of allosteric inhibitors for PTP1B, four example, MSI-1436, which primarily targets a different site in the disordered C-terminus (Krishnan et al., 2014).
evidence: Cites Krishnan et al., 2014 as evidence.

claim: RT fragments are also bound in the active-site pocket.
source: In addition to these three surface allosteric sites in the catalytic domain, we also see fragments bound in the active-site pocket (Pedersen et al., 2004).
evidence: States this as a result and cites Pedersen et al., 2004.

claim: In all four key sites (active site, BB site, 197 site, L16 site), fragments are observed that either adopt different poses at RT vs. cryo, or were not previously bound in that site at all at cryo.
source: Notably, in all four of these key sites, we observe fragments that either adopt different poses at RT vs. cryo, or were not previously bound in that site at all at cryo (Figure 3).
evidence: States this as a result and references Figure 3.

claim: Novel ligand poses in sites that are known to harbor allosteric capability offer promising new routes for fragment-based drug design.
source: Such novel ligand poses in sites that are known to harbor allosteric capability offer promising new routes for fragment-based drug design (Krojer et al., 2020).
evidence: Infers this from the results and cites Krojer et al., 2020.

claim: Fragment-based drug design could be done either by 'growing' existing inhibitors by attaching moieties similar to fragment poses, or by designing new inhibitors 'from scratch' by identifying compounds that combine the poses of multiple fragments in a site.
source: This could be done either by 'growing' existing inhibitors by attaching moieties similar to fragment poses, or by designing new inhibitors 'from scratch' by identifying compounds that combine the (new) poses of multiple fragments in a site (Gahbauer et al., 2023).
evidence: Describes potential drug design strategies and cites Gahbauer et al., 2023.

claim: Fragment poses for drug design could derive from previous cryo structures and/or new RT structures; the merits of combining multiple such sources of poses remain to be explored.
source: Fragment poses for these designs could derive from previous cryo structures and/or our new RT structures; the merits of combining multiple such sources of poses remain to be explored.
evidence: Speculates on the potential for combining cryo and RT data.

claim: Fragment-based design strategies could be used to develop non-covalent allosteric modulators or, in the case of the 197 site, covalent allosteric modulators of the WT enzyme.
source: Fragment-based design strategies could be used to develop non-covalent allosteric modulators or, in the case of the 197 site as mentioned above, covalent allosteric modulators of the WT enzyme (Figure 9).
evidence: Speculates on the potential for drug development and references Figure 9.

claim: A fragment binds at a new site at RT: the N-terminal α1'-α2' helical bundle, corresponding to an allosteric inhibitor binding site in SHP2.
source: In addition to the fragments at previously established binding sites in PTP1B, as noted above we also see a fragment bound at a new site at RT: the N-terminal α1'-α2' helical bundle, corresponding to an allosteric inhibitor binding site in SHP2 (Chen et al., 2016; LaRochelle et al., 2018).
evidence: States this as a result and cites Chen et al., 2016 and LaRochelle et al., 2018.

claim: The N-terminal α1'-α2' helical bundle site was not bound by any fragments in the previous cryo screen.
source: This site was not bound by any fragments in the previous cryo screen (Keedy et al., 2018), making this new fragment a potentially valuable starting point for exploring the possible allosteric capabilities of this relatively underexplored region of the PTP1B catalytic domain tertiary structure.
evidence: Cites the previous study as evidence.

claim: The new fragment bound at the N-terminal α1'-α2' helical bundle is a potentially valuable starting point for exploring the possible allosteric capabilities of this relatively underexplored region of the PTP1B catalytic domain tertiary structure.
source: This site was not bound by any fragments in the previous cryo screen (Keedy et al., 2018), making this new fragment a potentially valuable starting point for exploring the possible allosteric capabilities of this relatively underexplored region of the PTP1B catalytic domain tertiary structure.
evidence: Infers this from the result.

claim: Most AI/ML methods for protein structure prediction and drug design rely on training data in the form of experimental protein structures from the PDB, the vast majority of which are cryo temperature crystal structures.
source: More relevant to the work reported here, AI/ML is being used to great effect for SBDD and computational chemistry, including protein-ligand docking (Corso et al., 2022) and ligand design (Wallach et al., 2015). Importantly, all of these methods rely on training data in the form of experimental protein structures from the PDB, the vast majority of which are cryo temperature crystal structures.
evidence: States this as a fact about AI/ML methods and cites relevant work.

claim: For structure prediction, the temperature distribution of training data undoubtedly introduces bias into the predicted models, likely favoring well-packed states that preclude functionally required conformational heterogeneity.
source: For structure prediction, this temperature distribution undoubtedly introduces bias into the predicted models, likely favoring well-packed states that preclude functionally required conformational heterogeneity.
evidence: Infers this from the predominance of cryo structures in the PDB.

claim: For drug design, the temperature distribution of training data may favor protein-ligand interactions that overweight enthalpic considerations and underweight entropic ones, feature inaccurate solvation environments, or suggest artificially rigid proteins.
source: For drug design, it may favor protein-ligand interactions that overweight enthalpic considerations and underweight entropic ones, feature inaccurate solvation environments, or suggest artificially rigid proteins.
evidence: Infers this from the predominance of cryo structures in the PDB.
